decision.location: Section 1.2 Empirical Foundations, pp. 1-2 (and Reference 4, p. 15)
decision.quote: Dzulkifli and Mustafar (2013), in a widely-cited study, demonstrated that coloured backgrounds significantly enhanced recognition memory for geometric shapes compared to monochrome backgrounds, and that this effect was larger for warm colour conditions than cool colour conditions. Their work suggested that colour priming i.e., background colour presentation preceding or accompanying a cognitive task, could enhance memory retention through emotional arousal [4].
decision.reason: Matthew and Rakesh (2025) repeatedly claim to conduct a direct replication of a 2013 study by Dzulkifli and Mustafar that purportedly demonstrated enhanced recognition memory for geometric shapes on warm versus cool and monochrome coloured backgrounds, yet their sole citation [4] is the narrative review article 'The influence of colour on memory performance: A review' (Malaysian Journal of Medical Sciences, 20(2), 3; PMC3743993). Direct inspection of the complete text of Dzulkifli and Mustafar (2013) confirms that it synthesizes other authors' experiments (such as Pan, 2010, 2012; Greene et al., 1983; Spence et al., 2006; Smilek et al., 2002; McConnohie, 1999; Lloyd-Jones & Nakabayashi, 2009) and reports no primary empirical experiment of its own, despite thanking experiment participants in its acknowledgments. Moreover, the present 60-participant experiment administers PEBL digit/spatial working-memory span (MSPAN) and sustained-attention (TOAV) tasks, and neither the primary text nor the 2013 review identifies any published empirical study that tested those tasks or the attributed warm-versus-cool geometric-shape recognition experiment. Because a review article cannot be certified as an empirical target original and no underlying empirical study may be invented from topical similarity, the original study identity is undeterminable from the reported evidence.

decision.quote: This direct replication of Dzulkifli and Mustafar (2013) failed to detect significant effects of colour priming on memory span or sustained attention in a sample of 60 Indian university undergraduates. Warm colour (red) background did not enhance cognitive performance relative to cool colour (blue) or white control conditions. Effect sizes were negligible (η² < .053), substantially smaller than would be predicted from the original study or from theoretical models of colour-arousal effects on cognition.
decision.reason: Under the codebook, replication outcome evaluates whether the replication's results confirm or disconfirm the specific tested empirical finding of an identified target original study. Although Matthew and Rakesh (2025) report null differences across red, blue, and white background conditions on MSPAN memory span (χ²(2) = 0.808, p = .668) and TOAV sustained attention (p > .35) and frame these results as a failed direct replication of Dzulkifli and Mustafar (2013), the cited 2013 article is a narrative review that reports no primary empirical experiment or finding of its own, and no genuine underlying published empirical finding retested by the 60-participant MSPAN/TOAV task can be identified in either the primary source or the 2013 review. Consequently, a failed outcome cannot be certified for the shipped review citation or for an unidentifiable empirical original.

decision.quote: This study conducted a direct replication of Dzulkifli and Mustafar (2013) in an Indian university population. Sixty undergraduate students (ages 18–25) were randomly assigned to three conditions: warm colour (red; n = 20), cool colour (blue; n = 20), or white control (n = 20). Participants completed a digit memory span task (MSPAN) and a sustained attention task (TOAV).
decision.reason: Although the authors collect new experimental data from 60 Indian university undergraduates randomly assigned to warm (red), cool (blue), or white screen backgrounds on PEBL MSPAN and TOAV tasks and frame the study throughout as a 'direct replication of Dzulkifli and Mustafar (2013)', the codebook defines 'replication' as re-testing an earlier published empirical claim with new data and specifies that citing a review without re-testing an identifiable primary empirical study is 'not_a_replication'. Because the sole cited target [4] (Dzulkifli & Mustafar, 2013) is a narrative review that reports no primary experiment of its own (while thanking experiment participants in its acknowledgments) and neither the attributed geometric-shape recognition experiment nor any published empirical study matching the present MSPAN/TOAV tasks is identifiable in the source or the review, the source evidence is genuinely ambiguous as to whether an identifiable published empirical finding was actually retested.

decision.quote:
Nevertheless, what remains difficult to understand is why the targeted
COMT
-X-disorganization interaction only predicted change over time in the original Norwegian research and not levels of child behavior at either 4 or 6 years. Here, though, we found in our primary analyses that when disorganization was (a) measured categorically rather than continuously, (b) using the gold-standard Strange Situation rather than a story-stem completion task, and (c) at 15 months rather than at 4 years of age, that levels of kindergarten social behavior reported (only) by mothers could be accounted for by considering the moderation by
COMT
of attachment disorganization. Quite conceivably, these measurement and design differences across studies are responsible for the differences in findings across the two studies.
In any event, reasonably consistent support for the Norwegian hypothesis emerged in both inquiries as to why some children with disorganized attachment histories behave in seemingly controlling-caregiving and others in controlling-punitive ways. Especially notable, perhaps, is that in both studies the genetically-related divergent patterns of functioning are restricted to maternal reports of child behavior, thereby underscoring the relationship-specificity of disorganized attachment, at least when examined from the perspective of a gene -X-disorganization interaction.
decision.reason: Both the shipped row and blind coding record 'successful' by treating the authors' statements of support for 'the Norwegian hypothesis' as an unqualified Rule 1 whole-original replication verdict. However, in both the Introduction and the primary/sensitivity Discussion, Li et al. (2016) explicitly distinguish Hygen et al.'s (2014) initial theoretical hypothesis from Hygen et al.'s actual empirical findings: in Hygen et al. (2014), the COMT x attachment disorganization interaction predicted only change in social behavior from age 4 to 6 and did not predict levels of child behavior at age 4 or 6, whereas Li et al. (2016) tested and found the COMT x disorganization interaction for levels of social functioning (at kindergarten and Grade 6), explicitly acknowledging 'the differences in findings across the two studies' (alongside sensitivity analyses indicating a linear 3-level gene effect rather than Hygen et al.'s nonlinear 2-level pattern). At the same time, Li et al. confirm Hygen et al.'s empirical pattern of divergent maternal-reported positive and negative behavior between disorganized Met carriers and Val/Val homozygotes, absence of genetic differences among organized children, and relationship specificity to maternal rather than teacher reports. Because agreement with an original hypothesis does not override the authors' explicit contrast between the original change-only/null-levels finding and the present levels finding, aggregating the confirmed and contrasting original-specific empirical comparisons yields 'mixed'.

decision.location: Introduction and Materials and methods: Participants, line 4
decision.quote: Although we do not have previous genetic research to base our hypotheses on, based on clinical experiences, information processing theories in depression and the research by Seidel and colleagues [ 42 ], we expected avoidance of negative (sad, angry) facial expressions in remitted depressed S/L g -carriers who have experienced childhood trauma, as this represents the most vulnerable subgroup. Following Culverhouse and colleagues [ 9 ], we expected a main effect of childhood trauma on automatic approach-avoidance tendencies in depression. Materials and methods Participants This study is part of the ‘Info in Genes’ study, which involves a total of 337 remitted depressed patients. In the ‘Info in Genes’ study, the role of cognitive biases and genetic susceptibility to depression is investigated by assessing biased processing in several domains in remitted depressed patients [ 20 , 21 , 22 ].
decision.reason: Shipped row 937 (the sole shipped row for this paper) lists Vrijsen et al. (2014) [20] as the target original, and the initial expert retained it based on the broad Discussion sentence stating that the study 'partly supports earlier G x E findings... [ 10 , 11 , 14 , 16 – 22 ]'. However, the full text establishes that: (1) this study is part of the same 'Info in Genes' cohort of 337 remitted depressed patients as Vrijsen et al. [20, 21, 22], which assessed other cognitive-bias domains in that cohort and provided the childhood-trauma coding; (2) the citation range [10, 11, 14, 16–22] mixes theoretical reviews ([11, 14]), community attention studies, and same-programme papers without retesting any specific published empirical finding of Vrijsen et al. (2014); and (3) the authors explicitly state that their 5-HTTLPR x childhood trauma objective on the Approach-Avoidance Task (AAT) is tested for the first time here ('To our knowledge, the current study is the first study with this objective'; 'we do not have previous genetic research to base our hypotheses on'). The actual published empirical AAT finding in depression that the authors explicitly base their directional prediction on and test against their data is Seidel et al. (2010) [42] (automatic avoidance of angry faces in depression), matching blind target 0 and resolving the dependent target binding on row 937.

decision.quote: In line with Seidel and colleagues [ 42 ], we expected automatic avoidance of angry faces as well. We did not find this, however. The present results are tentative, but perhaps the signaling of sad rather than angry expressions is most relevant for depression. This would correspond with information processing models in depression: Sad faces are congruent to depressed patients’ mood state, activating depressotypic schemas, which lead to biased processing.
decision.reason: With row 937's target original resolved to Seidel et al. (2010) [42], the specific published empirical finding retested on the Approach-Avoidance Task is automatic avoidance of angry facial expressions in depression ('Seidel and colleagues [ 42 ], for example, found that depressed patients showed automatic avoidance in response to angry faces'). In the present study, there was no main effect of facial expression (F(3,201) = .30, p = .827) and no 5-HTTLPR x childhood trauma interaction for angry faces (F(1,203) < .01, p = .964, ηp² < .001), and the authors explicitly state in the Discussion that 'In line with Seidel and colleagues [ 42 ], we expected automatic avoidance of angry faces as well. We did not find this, however.' The novel 5-HTTLPR x childhood trauma interaction on sad faces (including the unexpected avoidance difference in LaLa homozygotes without versus with trauma) and generic support for broad GxE intermediate-phenotype theory concern the new genetic/trauma extension and do not make the replication of Seidel et al. (2010) mixed.
